For example, Yan et al. reported that, in ferromagnetic-element-based single-atom
catalysts, spin density is key factors governing the kinetics of the Li S → Li S
2 2 2
reduction.[1] In particular, Fe-N sites with higher spin polarization exhibit the lowest
4

2
17

3

and energy-level upshifts, which significantly enhance polysulfide adsorption,
accelerate sulfur conversion, and ultimately improve electrochemical performance.[2]
In addition, Zhang et al. found that, under an external magnetic field, Co atoms in
CoS systems undergo a transition from low-spin to high-spin states, generating more
x

2-x 2-x
exhibit excellent electrocatalytic activity.[4] The high-spin Co atoms contribute unpaired

hybridization with polysulfides, effectively suppressing the shuttle effect and
enhancing polysulfide conversion kinetics.
Moreover, similar spin-related catalytic trends have also been observed in a variety
of heterostructure materials.[5] As pointed out by your suggestion, this is indeed an
important direction that merits further exploration. For clarity and comparison, we have
systematically summarized representative studies in Supplementary Table 9.
Although numerous studies have addressed the sluggish kinetics of the SRR from
different perspectives, systematic investigations that clarify both why the rate-
determining step is intrinsically sluggish and how the catalyst spin moment
fundamentally regulates SRR kinetics remain limited. Addressing this gap is crucial for
establishing a solid physical foundation for spin-regulated sulfur redox catalysis.
In this study, our focus is to elucidate the mechanistic origin of the rate-determining
step associated with the Li S to Li S conversion in Li-S batteries. Theoretical
2 2 2
calculation reveal that this rate-determining step intrinsically involves a spin-state
transition-from a non-spin-polarized Li S /Li S initial-final state pair to a spin-
2 2 2
polarized reaction intermediate. This spin-state mismatch requires the reaction to
overcome an additional spin-flip barrier, thereby leading to intrinsically sluggish
18
kinetics. This phenomenon has also been observed in other electrocatalytic reactions.
For example, in the electrochemical nitrate-to-ammonia reduction reaction, the spin-
state transition from paramagnetic NO to singlet NHO leads to intrinsically sluggish
reaction kinetics. To deal with the intrinsically sluggish kinetics of rate-determining
step, recent studies have demonstrated that, compared with single-metal active centers,
magnetic coupling between two metal centers (e.g., Ni-O-Fe[6] or Ti-O-Fe[7]) can trigger
quantum spin-exchange interactions. Such interactions establish efficient electron-
transport channels within the lattice and provide additional reaction pathways for spin-
dependent electrocatalytic processes, thereby further accelerating reaction rates. This
strategy has been successfully validated in a variety of catalytic systems, where sluggish
kinetics similarly originate from spin-state transitions of reaction intermediates.
Rational modulation of the catalyst magnetic moment can therefore effectively reduce
spin-related reaction barriers, significantly improve reaction kinetics, and stabilize key
intermediates. However, systematic investigations into the mechanistic role of spin-
moment regulation in Li-S battery chemistry remain largely unexplored.
In this work, MoS -one of the most widely studied layered transition-metal
2
dichalcogenides-was selected the model substrate. Guided by machine-learning
analysis, we systematically evaluated how intrinsic catalyst descriptors influence the
Gibbs free-energy change along the sulfur conversion pathway. Spin moment was
identified as the dominant descriptor affecting the rate-determining step barrier.
Therefore, we designed a set of ten representative bimetallic systems composed of five
typical transition metals, and established a clear negative correlation between their spin
moments and the rate-determining step free-energy barriers. Catalysts with larger spin
moments consistently exhibited lower barriers and faster reaction kinetics.
To validate this finding experimentally while minimizing synthetic complexity and
resource consumption, we synthesized several bimetallic MoS catalysts with distinct
2
spin-moment distributions and evaluated their electrochemical performance. The
experimental results were fully consistent with theory: catalysts with larger spin
moments exhibited faster redox kinetics and significantly reduced reaction barriers,
19
thereby delivering superior Li-S battery performance.
To further understand how the catalyst spin moment influences the Li S to Li S
2 2 2
conversion, we simulated the spin polarization states of Li S and Li S on MoS (spin-
2 2 2 2
inactive) and Co,Ni-MoS (spin-active). As shown in Figs. 3j-m, when Li S and Li S
2 2 2 2
interact with pristine MoS , the spin-up and spin-down DOS remain symmetric,
2
indicating a non-spin-polarized state. Thus, the intrinsic spin-state transition of Li S to
2 2
Li S persists, leading to slow rate-determining step kinetics. In contrast, when Li S and
2 2 2
Li S are adsorbed on Co,Ni-MoS , both species exhibit clear spin asymmetry. This
2 2
suggests that the rate-determining step transforms into a spin-to-spin conversion
process, which enables quantum spin-exchange interactions and opens efficient
channels for spin-electron transfer, thereby accelerating the electrocatalytic conversion.
These results collectively demonstrate that the spin moment of the catalyst plays a
central role in facilitating the rate-determining step in Li-S batteries, ultimately
enhancing the electrochemical performance.
Establishing the universality of this linear relationship requires validation across a
broader range of catalyst systems. We are currently extending the study to additional
catalyst substrates and bimetallic configurations to further examine the generality of the
spin moment-activity correlation. Within the scope of the present work, our results
demonstrate that, for bimetallic-doped MoS catalysts, the spin moment serves as a
2
physically meaningful descriptor governing the rate-determining Li S and Li S
2 2 2
conversion. Your comments have been helpful in clarifying the scope of the present
work and in identifying meaningful directions for future study.

Comment #1: In fact, the 1T phase of MoS2 has a magnetic moment, while the 2H
phase has no single electron. This article should indicate which item the calculated and
prepared MoS2 belongs to, as well as whether the phase changes after diatomic
doping.
Response: Thank you for your suggestions. Indeed, the magnetic characteristics of
MoS are strongly correlated with its crystal phase: metallic 1T-MoS exhibit magnetic
2 2
moments, whereas intrinsically 2H-MoS is non-magnetic stable configuration. This
2
distinction is fundamental for clarifying the origin of spin polarization in our work, and
we appreciate you for highlighting this point. Although the metallic 1T phase may
exhibit spin-related properties, it is thermodynamically metastable and is generally
34
obtained through external treatments such as chemical activation or intercalation. This
intrinsic instability poses significant challenges for the precise and controllable
regulation of spin states in practical applications. Accordingly, the present study does
not rely on structural phase transitions to introduce magnetism; instead, it focuses on
achieving controllable spin polarization within the thermodynamically stable 2H lattice
via electronic structure reconstruction.
To address this concern experimentally, we carefully examined whether dual-metal
doping could induce a 2H to 1T phase transition in our synthesized catalysts. As shown
in Fig. 2i, the XRD pattern of pristine MoS displays distinct characteristic reflections
2
that match well with the standard 2H-MoS reference (JCPDS 37-1492), including
2
(002), (100), (103), and (110) planes. After Co-Ni incorporation, the doped MoS
2
samples exhibit XRD patterns that remain fully consistent with the same JCPDS card,
with no characteristic signatures of the metallic 1T phase. These results clearly confirm
that the 2H crystal phase is preserved after doping.
Furthermore, Raman spectroscopy further verifies the absence of a 2H to 1T phase
transformation. Both pristine MoS and dual-metal incorporation MoS display only the
2 2
signature E g1 and A g modes of the 2H phase, while no J /J /J vibrational fingerprints
2 1 1 2 3
corresponding to 1T phases are observed (Supplementary Fig. 20). The same Raman
profiles before and after doping demonstrate that dual-metal incorporation does not
induce a structural phase transition, but instead preserves the 2H lattice.
Therefore, the spin polarization observed in this work originates from localized
electronic reconstruction induced by Co-Ni dual-atom dopants, rather than a structural
phase transformation into the 1T phase. This demonstrates that spin modulation can be
achieved directly within the stable 2H lattice through targeted atomic engineering,
offering a more controllable and reliable strategy.
To maintain consistency with the experimental results, all DFT simulations in this
study were performed using the thermodynamically stable 2H-MoS structure, and no
2
1T-phase model was considered. The calculations were designed to examine whether
spin polarization can be induced within the conventional 2H lattice solely through
35
electronic reconstruction, without invoking any structural phase transition. This
clarification has now been explicitly added to the revised manuscript.
